title: One world, one Maker
source_text: Ἑξῆς τούτοις φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι τῷ ἡγησαμένῳ σφῶν ἑπόμενοι Μωϋσεῖ αἰπόλοι καὶ ποιμένες. ἀγροίκοις ἀπάταις ψυχαγωγηθέντες ἕνα ἐνόμισαν εἶναι θεόν. δεικνύτω τοίνυν πῶς, αἰπόλων καὶ ποιμένων ἀλόγως, ὡς οἴεται, ἀποστάντων τοῦ σέβειν θεοὺς. αὐτὸς δύναται παραστῆσαι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν καθ᾿ Ἕλληνας θεῶν ἢ τοὺς λοιποὺς βαρβάρους. δεικνύτω τοίνυν ὑπόστασιν καὶ οὐσίαν Μνημοσύνης γεννώσης ἀπὸ Διὸς τὰς Μούσας. ἢ Θέμιδος τὰς Ὥρας, ἢ τὰς Χάριτας ἀεὶ γυμνὰς παραστησάτω δύνασθαι κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ὑφεστηκέναι. ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δυνήσεται τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα σωματοποιεῖσθαι δοκοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων δεικνύναι θεούς. τί γὰρ μᾶλλον οἱ Ἑλλήνων μῦθοι περὶ θεῶν ἀληθεῖς ἢ, φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν, οἱ Αἰγυπτίων, οὐκ εἰδότων τῇ σφῶν διαλέκτῳ Μνημοσύνην μητέρα Μουσῶν ἐννέα οὐδὲ Θέμιν Ὡρῶν οὐδὲ Εὐρυνόμην μίαν τῶν Χαρίτων οὐδὲ τὰ λοιπὰ ὀνόματα αὐτῶν; πόσῳ οὖν ἐνεργέστερον καὶ πάντων τούτων τῶν ἀναπλασμάτων βέλτιον τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων πειθόμενον τοῖς κατὰ τὴν εὐταξίαν τοῦ κόσμου σέβειν τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτοῦ ἑνὸς ὄντος ἕνα καὶ συμπνέοντος αὐτοῦ ὅλῳ ἑαυτῷ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μὴ δυναμένῳ ὑπὸ πολλῶν δημιουργῶν γεγονέναι, ὡς οὐδ᾿ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ψυχῶν συνέχεσθαι ὅλον τὸν οὐρανὸν κινουσῶν· ἀρκεῖ γὰρ μία ἡ φέρουσα ὅλην τὴν ἀπλανῆ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἐπὶ δυσμὰς καὶ ἐμπεριλαβοῦσα ἔνδον πάντα. ὧν χρείαν ἔχει ὁ κόσμος, τὰ μὴ αὐτοτελῆ. πάντα γὰρ μέρη κόσμου, οὐδὲν δὲ μέρος ὅλου θεός· δεῖ γὰρ εἶναι τὸν θεὸν μὴ ἀτελῆ. ὥσπερ ἐστὶ τὸ μέρος ἀτελές. τάχα δὲ βαθύτερος λόγος δείξει ὅτι κυρίως θεὸς ὥσπερ οὐκ ἔστι μέρος οὕτως οὐδὲ ὅλον, ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅλον ἐκ μερῶν ἐστι· καὶ οὐχ αἱρεῖ λόγος παραδέξασθαι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν εἶναι ἐκ μερῶν. ὧν ἕκαστον οὐ δύναται ὅπερ τὰ ἄλλα μέρη.
pass_a_gloss: Next to these Celsus says that following (ἕπομαι) Moses who led (ἡγέομαι) them, goatherds (αἰπόλοι) and shepherds (ποιμένες), led on/beguiled (ψυχαγωγέω, aor. pass.) by rustic deceptions (ἄγροικοι ἀπάται), thought (νομίζω) there is one God. Let him show (δείκνυμι, impv.) then how, goatherds and shepherds having stood away (ἀφίστημι) irrationally (ἀλόγως), as he thinks, from worshipping (σέβω) gods, he himself is able to establish (παρίστημι) the multitude (πλῆθος) of gods according to the Greeks, or the remaining barbarians. Let him show the subsistence (ὑπόστασις) and substance (οὐσία) of Mnemosyne begetting (γεννάω) from Zeus the Muses, or of Themis the Hours (Ὧραι), or let him establish that the Graces (Χάριτες), always naked (γυμναί), can have subsisted (ὑφίστημι, pf.) according to substance. But he will not be able to show the fictions (ἀναπλάσματα) of the Greeks, seeming to be embodied (σωματοποιέω), from the facts (πράγματα) [to be] gods. For why are the myths (μῦθοι) of the Greeks about gods truer rather than, say (φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν), those of Egyptians, who do not know in their own dialect (διάλεκτος) Mnemosyne mother of nine Muses, nor Themis [mother] of the Hours, nor Eurynome one of the Graces, nor their remaining names? How much more effective (ἐνεργέστερον) then and better than all these fictions [is] the [act of] one persuaded (πείθομαι) from things seen (τὰ ὁρώμενα) by the features of the good order (εὐταξία) of the world (κόσμος) to worship its craftsman (δημιουργός) as one, it being one and breathing together (συμπνέω) with its whole self, and for this reason not able to have come into being (γίνομαι) from many craftsmen, as also not to be held together (συνέχω) by many souls (ψυχαί) moving the whole heaven (οὐρανός); for one suffices (ἀρκεῖ), the [soul] carrying (φέρω) the whole fixed [sphere] (ἀπλανής) from east (ἀνατολαί) to west (δυσμαί) and embracing within (ἐμπεριλαμβάνω) all things which the world needs (χρεία), the things not self-complete (αὐτοτελής). For all are parts (μέρη) of the world, but God is no part of a whole (ὅλον); for God must be not incomplete (ἀτελής), as the part is incomplete. Perhaps a deeper account (βαθύτερος λόγος) will show that God in the proper sense (κυρίως), as he is not a part, so neither a whole, since the whole is from parts; and reason does not allow/prove (αἱρέω) to accept (παραδέχομαι) the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) to be from parts, each of which cannot [do] what the other parts [can].
pass_b_english: Next Celsus says that "the goatherds and shepherds who followed Moses as their leader were beguiled by rustic deceits and came to think there is one God." Since, as he thinks, goatherds and shepherds turned away from the worship of gods without reason, let him show, then, how he himself can establish the multitude of gods held by the Greeks, or by the other barbarian peoples. Let him show the real existence and substance of Mnemosyne bearing the Muses by Zeus, or of Themis bearing the Hours; or let him prove that the Graces, who are always naked, can truly exist in substance. But he will not be able to show from the facts that the inventions of the Greeks, which seem to be given bodily form, are gods. Why are the Greeks' myths about gods any truer than, say, those of the Egyptians? In their own language the Egyptians know nothing of Mnemosyne as mother of the nine Muses, nor of Themis as mother of the Hours, nor of Eurynome as one of the Graces, nor any of their other names.

How much more effective, then, and how much better than all these inventions it is to be persuaded by what we see, by the good order of the world, to worship its Maker as one, since the world is one and wholly in harmony with itself! For that reason it cannot have been made by many makers, just as it cannot be held together by many souls moving the whole heaven. For one soul is enough, which carries the whole sphere of the fixed stars from east to west and embraces within it all the things the world needs, things that are not complete in themselves. For all these are parts of the world, but God is no part of a whole, since God cannot be incomplete, as a part is incomplete. Yet perhaps a deeper account will show that God, in the proper sense, is not a whole either, just as he is not a part, since a whole is made up of parts. And reason does not allow us to accept that the God over all is made up of parts, each of which cannot do what the other parts do.

choices.choice: Celsus's sentence is reported with ὅτι and keeps his wording, so it is put in quotation marks. The genealogies are Hesiodic (Theogony: Muses born of Mnemosyne by Zeus; Hours of Themis; Graces of Eurynome); not given inline because Origen alludes rather than quotes. The text reads Εὐρυνόμην μίαν τῶν Χαρίτων ('Eurynome one of the Graces'), whereas Hesiod makes Eurynome the Graces' mother; translated as transmitted, possible corruption. ἢ τοὺς λοιποὺς βαρβάρους construed loosely as 'or [those] of the other barbarians'. μία ('one', feminine) supplied as 'one soul' from ψυχῶν just before. ἀπλανής rendered 'sphere of the fixed stars'. The TEI full stops after Μούσας, ὑφεστηκέναι, πάντα, ἀτελῆ and μερῶν are construed across. Possible echo of Wisdom 13:1–5 or Romans 1:20 (knowing the Maker from visible things), too general to cite inline.
reordered stiff 'let him show, since ..., how' into natural English order
'bearing the Muses to Zeus' -> 'by Zeus' (ἀπὸ Διός)
restored dropped γάρ: 'For one soul is enough'
πάντα refers to the non-self-complete things: 'all things' -> 'all these'
modality: 'God must not be incomplete' (reads as prohibition) -> 'God cannot be incomplete' (δεῖ ... μὴ ἀτελῆ)
Eurynome 'one of the Graces' kept as transmitted; note already flags the Hesiodic 'mother'
